The 2025 RTP included the entire 765-kV STEP in its 2030 and 2031 starting base cases to address
base case violations and found it provided continued benefits in addressing new load growth. The
2025 RTP did not see a need to change or remove any element of the 765-kV STEP.

3.1.2   West Texas Study Findings

As described in Section 2.1, the Permian Basin load forecast from the S&P Global Commodity Insights
study was adopted in the 2025 RTP, similar to the 2021-2024 RTPs. This projected oil and gas load,
along with large loads seeking interconnections, increased the Far West load to nearly 19 GW by 2030
and nearly 20 GW by 2031 under summer peak conditions. In comparison, the 2029 summer peak
load forecast for the Far West Weather Zone was under 15 GW in the 2023 RTP. The 2025 RTP
incorporated the Permian Basin Reliability Plan local projects needed by 2030 that were approved by
the PUCT in September 2024. The 2025 RTP also included the three 765-kV import paths identified
by the Permian Basin Reliability Plan and approved by the PUCT in April 2025. The full Permian Basin
Reliability Plan, both local projects and import paths, were included in the 2030 and 2031 summer
peak cases.
3.1.3   Central Texas Study Findings

It was observed in the 2023 RTP that conventional Generation Resource retirements in and around
the San Antonio area contributed to stress on the existing 345-kV Central Texas corridor as new
renewable Generation Resources in the South Weather Zone made their way up to support load
growth in the South Central Weather Zone. In the 2024 RTP, generation in both the South and South
Central Weather Zones increased compared to the 2023 RTP cycle.

Despite generation increases in the South and South Central Weather Zones, the increase in large
load interconnection requests outpaced the generation growth. The new large load pockets in the
South and South Central Weather Zones have changed the flow patterns from what was observed in
the 2023 RTP. The trends seen in the 2024 RTP continued in the 2025 RTP. There was an addition
of approximately 12.8 GW of load in the 2031 summer peak case in the Central Texas corridor counties
of Bastrop, Bell, Bexar, Caldwell, Comal, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Hays, Medina, Milam, Travis, and
Williamson. The approximate large load concentration by county is illustrated in Figure 14.

Renewable resources in the South Weather Zone are now exporting less power to the San Antonio
and Austin areas with the increase of large loads in Calhoun, Nueces, and Cameron counties.
However, Central Texas faces the challenge of needing additional import capability. To meet the
higher projected load demand in Central Texas, new flow patterns have emerged, with imports to
Central Texas coming from north of Austin and the Coast Weather Zone.

Like the 2024 RTP, the 2025 RTP showed a need for additional import capacity along the pathway
from north of Austin to Central Texas as illustrated by Figure 15. A combination of upgrades along the
north-south corridor and new east-west 345-kV lines connecting Sandow Switch to Hutto are needed
to resolve the reliability violations in the northern area of Central Texas. A need to have more 345/138-
kV transformer capacity in Central Texas to serve the load at the 138-kV voltage level was also
observed in both the 2024 and 2025 RTPs.

 The reinforcement and expansion of the northern Central Texas import corridor alone is not sufficient
to address the issues identified in Central Texas. Strained import capability into the area was first
identified in the 2023 RTP, when it developed a South to Central Texas 345-kV import path extending
from the Corpus Christi area into Central Texas. However, with the dramatic increase in loads in the
Corpus Christi area in the 2024 RTP, there was less generation available for export. Instead, the 2024
RTP reinforced the existing 345-kV import corridors from Coast to South Central. The two import paths
coming from the Coast Weather Zone to Central Texas currently consist of lower-rated 345-kV lines
which limit the power transfer capability into the area to a level below what's needed. These two paths
are illustrated in Figure 16.

The expansion of the existing 345-kV Euclid station in Central Texas to include 765-kV helps stabilize
bus voltages and provides a new source into the Central Texas area, while the approximately 130 mile
Euclid to Hillje 765-kV line addresses various violations along the Coast-to-Central paths. Adding a
new 765-kV Central Texas import pathway from the Hillje substation in the Coast Weather Zone to the
Euclid station in Central Texas brings approximately 2,000 MW across the line into Central Texas
under base case summer peak conditions. The increased import capability is observed under both
normal and post-contingency conditions across various system topology configurations, including both



                                                                                                            -104-
                                                                                              Exhibit JG-R-3
                                                                                             Page 33 of 58




with the planned 765-kV STEP Eastern Backbone project and excusively on the new line's own merits
without the planned backbone as demonstrated in the early study years.

In addition to dramatically increasing overall import into the Central Texas area, the additional 765-kV
pathway will provide the much-needed operational flexibility for the system to handle any required
outage of those existing pathways without compromising system reliability.
The need for, and benefit from, this new 765-kV import path is seen as early as the 2027 study case.
However, the total system load in the 2027 study case, which includes TSP-submitted large loads
adjusted through the ETPALF process, is approximately 120,000 MW, approximately 35,000 MW
higher than the current summer peak demand record of 85,508 MW. The 2028 study case, with TSP-
submitted large loads, is approximately 140,000 MW, or 55,000 MW higher than the current summer
peak demand record.
Lastly, it is understood that the in-service date for a new 765-kV line would not be feasible by 2027.
However, based on those TSP-submitted load levels, an additional 765-kV import path was the best
solution to address the system needs identified at those particular load levels, independent of the in-
service timeline. Furthermore, similar alternative projects, including upgrading substantial miles of
345-kV lines or adding substantial new 345-kV Right-of-Way would experience similar in-service date
challenges. Therefore, the planning approach used in the 2025 RTP was to present the preferred
solution option. Should these system load levels materialize before the preferred transmission solution
is completed, the TSPs and ERCOT will work collaboratively to determine an appropriate CMP for the
operational situation at that time. Should those load levels materialize before the new import path is in
place, approximately 3,000 MW of future load would need to have its energization delayed based on
2027 study case load levels, and 6,000 MW of future load would need to have its energization delayed
based on 2028 study case load levels. Additional details can be found in Appendix G.

Detailed descriptions of all Central Texas area projects are in Appendix E. Expected future generation
and load will likely impact these needs, and therefore ERCOT and TSPs will continue to evaluate the
need and additional project options.
3.1.4   Other Findings

In addition to the reliability analysis summarized in previous sections, a multiple element outage
analysis was conducted for contingencies where non-consequential load loss is allowed under NERC
Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1, Table 1. This analysis consisted of:

    •   Corrective action analysis, which identified mitigation measures (such as transformer tap
        setting changes, switching actions, generator re-dispatch, and load shed) to resolve any
        overloads and over/under-voltage issues resulting from such contingencies; and
    •   Cascading analysis, which identified any contingencies that could result in potential cascade
        events.
Some planning events and extreme events were screened for detailed analysis, and further
investigation performed by ERCOT indicated that none of those events resulted in cascading



                                                - 105 -
                                                                                               Exhibit JG-R-3
                                                                                              Page 34 of 58




conditions. ERCOT also studied the loss of multiple generating stations due to the disruption of gas
pipelines. The results of the multiple element outage analysis are documented in Appendix H. This
appendix includes the list of critical contingencies identified as a result of this analysis and CAPs or
recommendations necessary to mitigate the impact of these contingencies.
ERCOT also performed an analysis of known outages of generation and transmission facilities planned
in the near-term planning horizon per Requirement 2.1.4 of NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1.
ERCOT issued Market Noticesl8 to collect known outages information from both TOs and GOs. TOs
were required to provide technical rationales fortheir selections of known outages for each study case
included in the 2025 RTP. ERCOT developed the technical rationale forthe selection of GO-submitted
outages to be included in the corresponding study cases. The known outages from the TOs and the
GO outages selected based on the ERCOT-developed technical rationale were then incorporated into
the base cases to study their impact on system performance under PO and Pl contingencies. The
study results found one additional violation was caused by the known outages. The CAP developed
to address this violation was project 2016- N01 - Kiamichi Energy Facility ( 140077) 345- kV Reactors
Addition , which was a CAP developed in the 2024 RTP under different system conditions . This CAP
has been developed in many previous RTPs since 2016. Additionally, there is currently an active
mitigation plan in ERCOT Operations to address the conditions observed that resulted in the CAP
during the known outages analysis. When the RE performs the maintenance captured in this known
outage analysis, the mitigation plan may need to be activated.
In addition to the above analyses, per ERCOT Planning Guide Section 3.1.1.2(3), the 2025 RTP
analysis included a list of transmission facilities that were loaded above 95% of their applicable ratings
under normal and contingency events (i.e., loss of single generating unit, transmission circuit,
transformer, or common tower outage). This list is attached to the report as Appendix I.

3.2.        Sensitivity ("Overnight") Analysis

The unprecedented system load totals from the 2024 RTP that were again incorporated in the 2025
RTP necessitated going beyond the current planning practices to add generation to meet the demand.
Portions of this generation did not meet Planning Guide 6.9(1) requirements. Stakeholders again
raised the following two key questions in the 2025 RTP that were previously raised in the 2024 RTP:

       1.   How will system needs change if not all large loads materialize?

       2. What are the impacts of the added generation that do not meet Planning Guide 6.9(1)
            requirements on system needs?
A third key question was raised in the 2025 RTP:

       3. What are the impacts in the West and Far West Weather Zones of no solar and low wind
            system conditions?

The sensitivity analysis was designed to address the first and second key questions in the 2025 RTP,
as it was in the 2024 RTP. In the sensitivity analysis, all large loads substantiated by TSP officerletters
were reduced to zero and all generators not currently meeting Planning Guide 6.9(1) requirements
were taken offline. The sensitivity analysis was performed on the 2027 and 2030 summer peak cases
and the 2028 minimum load case. Despite reducing the load substantiated by TSP officer letters from
over 23 GW to zero, the key reliability needs identified in the base case reliability analysis remained
similar.
The 2028 minimum load case (the "Overnight Case") was designed to answer the third key question.
The Overnight Case represents a typical spring season overnight timeframe of approximately 2 a.m.
to 4 a.m., when the system load is at its lowest annual point and solarand batteries are not dispatching
at any level. A combination of dispatchable and wind generation is serving system load. Table 1 below
summarizes key assumptions of the Overnight Base (BASE) case and the Overnight Sensitivity (SEN)
case. The Overnight BASE case included Officer Letter large loads, generation that had not met the
Planning Guide 6.9(1) requirements, and had wind dispatched at a higher level. Whereas the
Overnight SEN case included only large loads with a signed interconnection agreement, generation
that had met Planning Guide 6.9(1) requirements, and had wind dispatched to a much lower level.

3.3.              Peak Net Load ("Sunset") Analysis and Minimum Deliverability

To meet the Minimum Deliverability criteria as required by Planning Guide 4.1.1.7, the 2025 RTP
developed a 2027 study case to represent "sunset" conditions typically found during the 7-8 p.m. time
period.
The battery dispatch of 56.9% was based on the capacity factor observed on October 10,2025, hour
ending (HE) 19 when ERCOT set a battery discharge record of 8,714 MW.

The study condition was further stressed by mimicking a high Southern wind export condition. The
wind and solar capacity factors used in the Sunset BASE case were from August 11,2023, HE20,
when real-time system conditions saw a 345-kV South Texas export line reach 123.2% under a
potential contingency loss. These stressful system conditions were similarto September 6,2023, when
ERCOT entered Energy Emergency Alert conditions. The purpose of this analysis was not to focus
solely on the South Texas export challenge because the future planning project to resolve that issue
has already been ERCOT RPG-approved and will be energized at the point in time at which this study
evaluates. Instead, this analysis was meant to capture what are still the most challenging operating
conditions when solar is very low, wind in the West and Far West is low, and wind in the Panhandle is
very low. These conditions resulted in generation from the Southern and Coast Weather Zones
needing to travel across the entire system, including to the West and Far West Weather Zones,
stressing many paths along the way.
The generation in this case includes only future generation that meets Planning Guide requirements
6.9(1). The load in this study case is approximately 106 GW and contains only large loads with signed
interconnection agreements. This case does not include Officer Letter loads. The system load level is

                                                                                             Exhibit JG-R-3
                                                                                            Page 38 of 58




95.8% of the summer peak load level found in the RTP Sensitivity BASE case discussed in Section
3.2. The Sensitivity BASE case was the starting point for the Sunset analysis since the Sensitivity
BASE case did not include Officer Letter loads and included only Planning Guide 6.9(1) generation.

Table 3 below summarizes the load and generation details of the Sunset Base (BASE) case and the
Sunset Minimum Deliverability (MIN DELIV) case. The Sunset BASE was developed with the load and
generation assumptions shown in Table 3, and then an N-1 contingency analysis was performed, and
projects were developed to resolve violations found. Then, analysis involving a prior outage of a
generator or 345/138-kV transformer followed by N-1 contingency conditions was performed, and
projects were developed to resolve issues found.
The Sunset BASE case with its N-1 projects and prior outage projects then had its generation updated
to reflect the Minimum Deliverability criteria to become the Sunset MIN DELIV case. The analysis was
then repeated on the adjusted Sunset MIN DELIV case. N-1 contingency analysis was performed, and
projects were developed to resolve the violations that resulted. This was followed by analysis involving
a prior outage of a generator or 345/138-kV transformer followed by N-1 contingency conditions.
Projects were developed to address newly identified issues.

The purpose of first making the Sunset BASE case secure under the above conditions was to ensure
the violations seen after making the Minimum Deliverability adjustments were a direct result of those
generation adjustments. Those generation adjustments included setting Generation Resources
utilizing combined cycle, steam turbine, combustion turbine, hydro, or reciprocating engine technology
to 100% of their output along with any Energy Storage Resource (ESR) with a duration greater than
or equal to two hours. For ESRs with a duration of less than two hours, a prorated deliverability was
ensured. The output of these generator types was then fixed and redispatch of those generator types
was not allowed. This contrasts with the Sunset BASE case, where dispatchable units were allowed
to reach 100% of their possible output, but with redispatch enabled, some units were curtailed to
prevent violations. This resulted in an effective dispatch of approximately 94% for dispatchable units
in the Sunset BASE case.

4. Economic Analysis

The 2025 RTP economicanalysis was performed using production cost simulation runs foryears 2027
and 2030. In the analysis, both the production cost savings test and the congestion cost savings test
were utilized. Through this assessment, ERCOT identified transmission congestion and tested various
transmission improvements to address the congestion in a cost-effective manner as defined by
ERCOT's economic planning criteria.

A transmission system upgrade is economically viable if it meets the 1) production cost savings test
requirement, or 2) congestion cost savings test requirement.
Twelve economic transmission improvement projects were evaluated in the 2025 RTP. Break-even
capital cost was provided for the projects that showed positive economic benefits.
Details of the economic analysis and project evaluation results can be found in Appendix P.

4.1.       Study Assumptions and Methodology

The 2025 RTP economic cases used the 2024 RTP final reliability cases as the start cases, specifically
the 2027 summer peak case and the 2030 summer peak case with the 765-kV - STEP incorporated.

4.1.1      Load and Generation Assumptions

Two sets of cases with different load and generation assumptions were developed for each study year
to demonstrate the system impact underdifferent forecasted load levels. The first set of cases included
both the large loads with a signed Interconnection Agreement and the large loads substantiated by
TSP Officer Letters with the PUCT-approved GCE applied20. This set of cases is referred to as base
cases in this report, and the resulting coincident peak for study year 2030 is approximately 123.6 GW.
The other set of cases included only the large loads with a signed Interconnection Agreement. This
set of cases is referred to as sensitivity cases in this report, and the resulting coincident peak for study
year 2030 is approximately 109.6 GW.

Similar to the reliability analysis, ERCOT took steps outside of the normal planning process to
incorporate more Generation Resources into the planning models used in the 2025 RTP economic
analysis based on the rules proposed by PGRR12721. PGRR127 modifies the criteria for adding
Generation Resources to the planning models and is currently going through the stakeholder process.
The generators were added in the sequence outlined below until there was sufficient generation to
meet the demand forall hours:
       •   Large generators that have a signed Standard Generation Interconnection Agreement
           submitted by the TSP via the online Resource Integration and Ongoing Operations system;
       •   Large generators that have completed the FIS; and
       •   Large generators that have started the FIS.

4.4.1   Top Constraints for Sensitivity Cases

The 2025 RTP economic analysis used the 2027 and 2030 sensitivity cases to assess the cost-
effectiveness of potential transmission improvements for top constraints. Brief descriptions of the top
congestion seen in these cases are presented below, and more details can be found in Appendix P.

In the West and Far West Weather Zones, the rapid growth in renewable generation is expected to
continue. Like the 2024 RTP economic analysis, the WTX interface was the most congested element
observed for both the 2027 and 2030 study years. The interface was congested approximately 24.1%
and 15.8% of hours in the 2027 and 2030 study years, respectively. The congestion rent on this
interface was $245 million in 2027. With the 765-kV STEP incorporated in the 2030 study case, the
congestion rent for the WTX interface remained high at $209 million. Opportunities for further
transmission investment to increase the interface limit should be monitored in the future as renewable
generation buildout continues in the West, Far West, and Panhandle regions.

The North to Houston interface26 showed a congestion rent of $48 million in 2027 and $141 million in
2030. The interface was congested 11.8% of hours in 2027 and 25.6% of hours in 2030 due to rising
energy demand in the greater Houston area.

The Panhandle area is also seeing continuous development of new renewable resources, resulting in
$12 million and $45 million congestion rent in 2027 and 2030, respectively, on the Panhandle interface.
Moreover, in the same area, the Wett Long Draw to Holly POI to Farmland 345-kV line was also among
the top constraints.
The Houdini to WA Parish 345-kV line was projected to incur high congestion rent in 2027 ($150
million). The congestion rent dropped to $22 million in 2030 with the 765-kV STEP incorporated. The
percentage of congestion time dropped from 24.3% of hours in 2027 to 6.7% of hours in 2030.

Based on the review of the initial congestion pattern and historical congestion, ERCOT selected
transmission projects to conduct both the production cost savings test and the congestion cost savings
test. A summary of the evaluated projects is provided in Section 4.5.

4.6.    Project Evaluation Results

Using the 2025 RTP sensitivity cases for both 2027 and 2030 study years, ERCOT performed an
economic analysis for 12 transmission enhancements chosen based on a review of the initial
congestion patterns and historical data.
Both the congestion cost savings test, measured by the system-wide consumerenergy cost reduction,
and the production cost savings test were performed in the project evaluation. The total production
cost is the sum of the fixed operation and maintenance (O&M), startup, variable O&M, fuel, and
emission cost of generators. The total consumer energy cost equals the sum of load payments for
energy use. To pass the production cost savings test, the Ievelized ERCOT-wide annual production
cost savings attributable to the proposed projectshould be equal to orgreaterthan the first-yearannual
revenue requirement (13.0%) of the proposed project. To satisfy the congestion cost savings test
requirement, the Ievelized ERCOT-wide annual consumer energy cost reduction attributable to the
proposed project should be equal to or greater than the average of the annual revenue requirement
for the first three years (12.7%) of the proposed project. These revenue requirements are reviewed
